paragraphs.source_en: Despite being a carefree teenager, I remember how the process of writing and posting a family mission statement made me feel. I was a vital part of my family, and we *did* have purpose. We were about something. And even though we had lots of problems and fights like every family does, it helped us create a resilient and fun family culture, where we enjoyed being together and where everyone was willing to apologize and try again.

paragraphs.source_en: Since then, I’ve seen many tremendous family mission statements. I have a good friend with four kids, and his family mission statement looks like a massive constitution hanging on his wall, with about two thousand words, for crying out loud! On the other hand, my aunt and uncle have a three-word mission statement: *No Empty Chairs*. And I have a Danish friend whose family has a single-word mission, which is the name of their family cabin, Helsifor. To them, it means everything.

paragraphs.source_en: ### ORGANIZATIONAL MISSION STATEMENTS—NOT JUST WORDS ON A WALL

units.source_en: ### ORGANIZATIONAL MISSION STATEMENTS—NOT JUST WORDS ON A WALL

ja.t: のミッション・ステートメント――

paragraphs.source_en: Organizational mission statements sometimes get a lot of flak because so often they’re just platitudes nobody lives by, or they’re created by a couple of people at corporate and pushed down the organization with no buyin. But you can’t underestimate the power of creating a mission as a team and getting it right. Some organizational mission statements are so genuine you can feel their mission exuding from their people, products, and services. Two that jump out at me are IKEA and American Girl. I’ve bought a lot of furniture from IKEA and dolls from American Girl, and their mission statements perfectly capture my experience with them.
